title: Katzmann: Purposivism, textualism, and legislative history (pp. 29–49)
shortTitle: Katzmann: Purposivism, textualism, and legislative history (pp. 29–49)
summary: Katzmann defends careful use of reliable legislative history while acknowledging textualism’s criticism of manipulation and indeterminate purpose.
notes:
Katzmann defines the judicial task as faithful interpretation of enacted legislation. He generally ends with unambiguous text and does not authorize judges to substitute preferred policy. For ambiguous language, he seeks the statute’s purposes and reliable evidence of the legislature’s work. His account connects Holy Trinity to the later legal-process approach of Hart and Sacks, whose purposive interpretation remained limited by meanings the words could bear and applicable clear-statement requirements.

The textualist critique has several forms: only enacted text passes bicameralism and presentment; committee materials may empower unrepresentative staff or members; inconsistent records may allow selective judicial reliance; and refusal to consult legislative history might encourage more precise drafting. Public-choice accounts of legislative bargaining helped motivate some criticism, although Katzmann notes a later emphasis on constitutional structure and the enacted terms of compromise. Modern textualists still use linguistic context, technical terms, and background conventions.

Katzmann answers that institutional purpose can exist despite different individual motives, that Congress uses legislative history for internal communication and agency guidance, and that excluding useful evidence may enlarge rather than constrain judicial discretion. He accepts that legislative materials can be manipulated and credits textualism with making courts more careful and text-centered. He disputes a universal assumption that eliminating history will remove ambiguity, given unavoidable complexity and strategic compromise. These are the author’s arguments in a 2014 book, not a census of current judicial methodology.
